title: ProAct: A Benchmark and Multimodal Framework for Structure-Aware Proactive Response
claim: Following the human's next step can block workflows; a task graph lets an agent pursue independent parallel actions instead.
layout: Top video timeline, task list left, task graph bottom, zoomed frame right
description: The figure opens with a Previous/Current/Future timeline bar above a strip of first-person video frames. The current frame is highlighted in blue and enlarged on the right, showing a person taking out an old garbage bag. At left, a gray-to-blue-to-green panel lists the five tasks: trigger detection, step detection, task detection, future action prediction and proactive action selection. Each task has a one-line description. The bottom shows a partial task graph with photo nodes. A human icon marks the current step. An orange node, labeled 'Blocking my way?', shows a robot tying the bag and getting in the person's way. A green node, labeled 'Parallel teamwork!', shows the robot taking out a new trash bag. An AND join leads to 'Leave with trash'. A legend identifies human steps and robot-selected actions. Curved arrows connect the task list to the graph.
caption: Overview of proactive response tasks. ProAct-75 supports five vision-based tasks with step-level annotations, hierarchical labels, and task graphs. Traditional intent-following approaches predict human-intended actions (\eg, tie the bag) and execute them, inadvertently blocking workflows. Our benchmark enables evaluation of strategies where robots pursue independent parallel threads to reduce disruptions.
abstract: While passive agents merely follow instructions, proactive agents align with higher-level objectives, such as assistance and safety by continuously monitoring the environment to determine when and how to act. However, developing proactive agents is hindered by the lack of specialized resources. To address this, we introduce ProAct-75, a benchmark designed to train and evaluate proactive agents across diverse domains, including assistance, maintenance, and safety monitoring. Spanning 75 tasks, our dataset features 91,581 step-level annotations enriched with explicit task graphs. These graphs encode step dependencies and parallel execution possibilities, providing the structural grounding necessary for complex decision-making. Building on this benchmark, we propose ProAct-Helper, a reference baseline powered by a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) that grounds decision-making in state detection, and leveraging task graphs to enable entropy-driven heuristic search for action selection, allowing agents to execute parallel threads independently rather than mirroring the human's next step. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ProAct-Helper outperforms strong closed-source models, improving trigger detection mF1 by 6.21%, saving 0.25 more steps in online one-step decision, and increasing the rate of parallel actions by 15.58%.
